Sampling We performed preliminary sampling on rocks span- ning a wide range of ages, locations, and structural orientations in northwestern Bulgaria (Fig. 1). Results reveal that the formations yielding the best results are of Triassic age, leading us to focus subsequent sampling on Upper Permian – Lower Triassic (‘‘Bundsandstein’’ red sandstone) and Middle – Upper Triassic (carbo- nates) units. In total, 8 sites (58 samples) in Lower Triassic, 19 sites (174 samples) in Middle – Upper Triassic, 1 site (14 samples) in Middle Jurassic, 4 sites (37 samples) in the Upper Jurassic, and 4 sites (34 samples) in the Lower Cretaceous rocks were obtained. The evolution of the deformation in this area was very different on either side of the present discontinuity. Thus, the deformation started along more or less parallel zones that possibly correspond to previous (sedimentary or tectonic) discontinuities. Around each ‘‘discontinuity’’, the overlying southern part acted as a rigid block, and the ‘‘folding’’ front advanced north- ward in the underlying northern part. Conclusion The characteristic component of magnetization (ChRM A) observed in Upper Permian – Lower Tri- assic sediments in northwestern Bulgaria is likely a primary direction. The orientation of a secondary component (ChRM B) is believed to reflect a clock- wise rotation of this area relative to stable Europe after the beginning of the main Middle Eocene tectonic phase. The ChRM B provides a unique picture of the geological structures at an intermediate stage of defor- mation, and reveals that Eocene deformation began in the south and proceeded northwards. Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). These bedded bodies rarely exceed more than tens of meters wide in length Fig. 3.

Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). These bedded bodies rarely exceed more than tens of meters wide in length Fig. 3.

At first glance, the M- JC district seems to provide a poor fit to this correlation because the Acadian and Alleghanian orogenies are thought to span from f 390 to f 350 and from f 320 to f 250 Ma, respectively (Hatcher et al., 1989; Gar- ven et al., 1993), leaving the 316 F 8 Ma ore-forming event just straddling the start of the Alleghanian oro- geny. Introduction The Mascot – Jefferson City Mississippi V alley- type (MVT) zinc deposits are located in the V alley and Ridge physiographic province of the Appalachian orogen in eastern Tennessee (Fig. 1). They have been in fairly continuous production since 1854, and were the main source of zinc for the USA from the mid- 1950s to about 1990, providing more than half of its production at times (Fulweiler and Hill, 1992). Brecciation The M-JC ore-bearing structures consist of two interrelated types of breccia bodies. ‘‘Breakthrough’’ structures cut one or more stratigraphic units. They are discordant bodies up to several thousand meters long, up to a few hundred meters wide, and up to >150 m high (Hoagland et al., 1965; Crawford et al., 1969). They may be V-shaped, low-domal or high- domal structures that appear to follow pre-mineralisa- tion faults and joints, and that are filled with a rubble breccia containing several petrographic types of clasts (McCormick et al., 1971; Hill, 1969; Hill et al., 1971a; Hoagland, 1976). Crackle breccias are found around the top and sides of the breakthrough struc- tures. The Immel, Young and New Market ore bodies are in ‘‘breakthrough’’ breccias. ‘‘Bedded’’ structures occur only within certain limestone beds in the King- sport Formation. They are semi-concordant tabular mantos of dolomitisation, brecciation and mineralisa- tion that appear to extend laterally from breakthrough breccia bodies in most cases (Kendall, 1960; Ful- weiler and McDougal, 1971). At first glance, the M- JC district seems to provide a poor fit to this correlation because the Acadian and Alleghanian orogenies are thought to span from f 390 to f 350 and from f 320 to f 250 Ma, respectively (Hatcher et al., 1989; Gar- ven et al., 1993), leaving the 316 F 8 Ma ore-forming event just straddling the start of the Alleghanian oro- geny. This is awkward because the M-JC ore-forming event is shown to be post-folding yet appears to occur almost at the start of the Alleghanian orogeny. The time span of the Acadian orogeny in the central Appalachian orogen is fairly consistently defined. In their summary article, Osberg et al. (1989) gave a span from f 415 to f 360 Ma with peak orogenesis at f 390 Ma based broadly on radiometric, metamor- phic, structural, and other evidence. Garven et al. (1993) set the limits at f 395 and f 350 Ma for the purpose of hydrologic modeling. Hamilton-Smith (1993) leaned heavily on sedimentological evidence and placed the limits at f 390 and f 360 Ma. art of the Kisseynew Domain of the Trans-Hudson Orogen (THO) in north-central Manitoba. The dome is circular, about 6 km in diameter, with steeply-dipping flanks. It is composed of upper amphibolite-facies gneisses derived from turbiditic sediments, with leucogranitic sill-like intru - sions that were metamorphosed, starting at about 1830 Ma. Alternating field and thermal step demagnetization of 153 specimens from 17 sites around the perimeter of the dome isolated a characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) di - rection of D = 346.6°, I = 78.9° ( a 95 = 5.3°, k = 46, N = 17) that gives a pole of 119.5° W, 75.8° N ( dp = 9.5°, dm = 10.0°). Unblocking temperatures and saturation isothermal remanence analyses show that the ChRM resides mostly in single to pseudosingle domain magnetite or titanomagnetite, with minor hematite commonly present and with minor pyrrhotite present in the leucogranites. The ChRM is found to be postfolding with >>99.9% confidence, indicating ac - quisition on cooling from peak metamorphism at ~1810 ± 10 Ma. This Wapisu gneiss dome paleopole is the first from the Kisseynew Domain and the first from the 1830 to 1770 Ma interval in the THO. It indicates an ~90° bend or hair - pin in the apparent polar wander path for the THO juvenile terranes and Superior craton. It is speculated

At 72% unfolding, the Williston paleopole is rotated by 10 ± 12° clockwise with respect to the Early Cretaceous North America reference paleopole (124–88 Ma) of Van Fossen and Kent (1992; latitude 71.2°N, longitude 194.1°E), whereas at 100% unfolding the Williston paleopole is rotated by 19 ± 10° counterclockwise from this reference pole. At 87% unfolding, where directional grouping is best, the angular distance between the Williston and Cretaceous reference paleopoles is 7.5 ± 9°, whereas at 80% unfolding the paleopoles are also statistically indistin - guishable (Fig. 8). We suggest that Triassic rocks at Williston Lake were remagnetized during the initial stages of the Cretaceous– Cenozoic Laramide orogenic phase between 72 and 100% unfolding. The exclusive occurrence of normal polarity directions can then be reconciled with remanence acquisition during either the Cretaceous long normal superchron, a period of the Earth’s magnetic field from about 118 to 84 Ma characterized by stable normal polarity, or perhaps one of the somewhat shorter, but still appreciable in length, normal polarity chrons in the Late Cretaceous (e.g., C33n). e.g., Ogg and Steiner 1991; Kent et al. 1995; Gallet et al. 1996, 1998; Muttoni et al. 1997). The most complete sequence of Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic magnetic polarity reversals comes from the Newark conti - nental rift basin succession of eastern North America (Kent et al. 1995), which led to the construction of the first reliable GPTS for 30 Ma of the Late Triassic (Kent and Olsen 1999). Triassic stage boundaries are, however, historically based on marine biostratigraphy, essentially from ammonoids and conodonts. We performed a paleomagnetic reconnaissance at three classic sections of Middle and Late Triassic marine fossiliferous limestones around Williston Lake in northeastern British Columbia. These sections have provided an integrated conodont–ammonoid biostratigraphic scale for the North America Triassic marine realm (Orchard and Tozer 1997). This study is aimed at testing the suitability of these sections for more detailed magnetostratigraphic study to correlate the marine biostratigraphic zonation to the nonmarine Newark reference GPTS. Therefore, all the palasomagnetic results will be presented in this paper only after dip correction. In Late Cretaceous times, greater India broke away from Madagascar with voluminous igneous activity accompanying the continental break-up. A geochemi- cal study of the Madagascan flood basalts suggests that the Marion hot spot was an important source of melts at the southern end of the island (Mahoney et a/., 1991; Storey et a/., 1997). This is also supported by a palaeogeographic reconstruction placing Mada- gascar in the near vicinity of the Marion hot spot around Late Cretaceous times (Storey et a/., 1995; Torsvik et a/., 1998). GEOLOGY OF NICARAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1

, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivision of the Coyol Group. To the west of the depression, in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain, the rocks are predominantly of sedimentary origin and are assumed to have been deposited on a Nicoya Complex type of basement (Parsons Corporation Report 1972). The sediments, tuffaceous shale, siltstone, greywacke, sandstone and lime- stone, range in age from Cretaceous to Miocene (Rivas, Brito, Masachapa and El Fraile formations) and are overlain by sediments of similar composition to the El Salto Formation and the pyroclastic deposits of the La Sierra Group (McBirney & Williams 1965; Parsons Corporation Report 1972). Seyfried et al. (1987) regard the Upper Cretaceous Rivas and the Eocene Brito formations as parts of a continuous succession. The Masachapa Formation is Oligocene in age (Auer 1942, unpublished paper; Zoppis Bracci & Del Guidice 1958) and the boundary between the Brito and Masachapa formations has been interpreted as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965). Also, the contact between the Masachapa Formation and the overlying Miocene El Fraile Formation is regarded as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965; Kuang 1971) and the El Fraile Formation interﬁngers with part of the volcanic Tamarindo Formation. - dominantly volcanic rocks from the Miocene Lower Coyol Group and from assumed Oligocene–Palaeocene rocks of the Matagalpa Group were sampled. As the tectonic control was often poor, our ambition has been to collect samples of rocks of similar age but geographically well-separated in order to detect later local tectonic movements. To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi- mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively. MINERALOGICAL STUDIES Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi 1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites. Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Alth

K–Ar AND 40 Ar / 39 Ar RADIOMETRIC AGE DETERMINATIONS In order to constrain the ages of magnetizations in this study, we have dated samples from selected palaeomagnetic sites by the K–Ar and 40Ar /39Ar methods. Previous Rb–Sr and K–Ar dating of whole-rock and mineral phases (Zoppis Bracci 1961; Barr & Escalante 1969; McBirney & Williams 1965) from both the Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain were of poor resolution and indicate that many of the units may have been emplaced over a long duration. Dating the same samples and ﬂows for which we have stable magnetic directions allows us to avoid assigning ‘incorrect’ or estimated ages to the magnetization. The K–Ar age determinations were made by R. M. Macintyre at the Scottish Universities Research and Reactor Centre (Table 1). One–four palaeomagnetic samples from each of the 11 sites 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16 and 17 were analysed, including andesite and basalt from the Lower Coyol and Matagalpa groups and a diabase dy

es 16 and 17) and three were chosen from other localities of the Matagalpa Group (sites 8, 12 and 14). Samples were crushed and sieved and small chips from the 100–250 mm fraction were chosen for dating. Samples of Bern4B biotite with an assumed age of 17.25t 0.20 Myr were used to monitor the neutron ﬂux. The samples were irradiated for 2 MW h in position 5c of the uranium-enriched research reactor of McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada. The samples were step-heated from about 500 to 1600 uC. The puriﬁed argon isotopes were then analysed in a Nuclide 6-60-SGA mass spectrometer at the Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, USA. Argon puriﬁcation was achieved using a liquid nitrogen cold trap SAES Zr–Al getter at 400 uC. The measured argon isotopes were corrected for system blank and mass discrimination as well as calcium, potassium and chlorine interference reactions following the procedures outlined in McDougall & Harrison (1988). Plateau ages were based on the criteria of three or more contiguous fractions accounting for more than 50 per cent gas release having ages within a 2s (95 per cent conﬁdence level) of the mean age. ical evidence, most of the samples dated by the 40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. If these signs of alteration are prevalent throughout the sample suite, then interpretation of the K–Ar ages is difﬁcult. Nevertheless, we can infer that the age of the Tamarindo Group of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain is c. 15 Myr, samples correlative with the Lower Coyol Group are c. 18 Myr, the La Batea member of the Matagalpa Formation is c. 20 Myr, Matagalpa sites 8, 9 and 12 are c. 24 Myr and sites 13 and 14 are c. 30 Myr. section_candidates.excerpt: RAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter- mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivis

Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Although the remanent magnetization of haematite is usually more resistant to demagnetization than magnetite, no signiﬁcant relation between degree of martitization and directional variations of the characteristic magnetizations was found. These rocks yield directions of magnetization (Fig. 6a) of reversed and dual polarities, signiﬁcantly different from those of the La Batea Formation. The declinations vary from c. 90u to 140uE and the inclinations are predominantly negative and lower than c. 30u. It is possible to distinguish two groups of directions with signiﬁcantly different declinations of c. 130uE (sites 8, 9 and 12) and 90uE (sites 13 and 14), respectively. The rocks of the two groups are sampled from geographically well-separated areas (Fig. 3). The coercivity of remanence of the ﬁrst group varies but the directions are fairly stable after being demagnetized in 10 mT AF. The rock at site 8 carries characteristic magnetizations of dual polarity, which may indicate that the rock at this site has not been remagnetized. As for the La Batea Formation the mean directions of the sites (Table 2) show that the inclinations are different while the declinations are quite similar. section_candidates.excerpt: RAGUA Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben (McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter- mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivis

As the tectonic control was often poor, our ambition has been to collect samples of rocks of similar age but geographically well-separated in order to detect later local tectonic movements. To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi- mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively. MINERALOGICAL STUDIES Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi 1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites. Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite, is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Alth

ical evidence, most of the samples dated by the 40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. If these signs of alteration are prevalent throughout the sample suite, then interpretation of the K–Ar ages is difﬁcult. Nevertheless, we can infer that the age of the Tamarindo Group of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain is c. 15 Myr, samples correlative with the Lower Coyol Group are c. 18 Myr, the La Batea member of the Matagalpa Formation is c. 20 Myr, Matagalpa sites 8, 9 and 12 are c. 24 Myr and sites 13 and 14 are c. 30 Myr. Age summary Based on our new geochronological evidence, most of the samples dated by the 40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivision of the Coyol Group. The Cocos Plate subducts below the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of the depression parallel to the trench. East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996). Ehrenborg (1996) has explained the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the older subdivision of the Coyol Group. Seyfried et al. (1987) regard the Upper Cretaceous Rivas and the Eocene Brito formations as parts of a continuous succession. The Masachapa Formation is Oligocene in age (Auer 1942, unpublished paper; Zoppis Bracci & Del Guidice 1958) and the boundary between the Brito and Masachapa formations has been interpreted as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965). Also, the contact between the Masachapa Formation and the overlying Miocene El Fraile Formation is regarded as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965; Kuang 1971) and the El Fraile Formation interﬁngers with part of the volcanic Tamarindo Formation. Also in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain secondary zeolite and clay minerals are found originating from alterations of volcaniclastics in the sedi- mentary units (Levi et al. 1990). The secondary minerals show a vertical zoning typical of burial diagenesis, which is a process controlled by an increase in temperature with depth. A palaeo- thermal gradient of about 15–20 uCk m x1 is estimated for the Cretaceous to Oligocene diagenetic episodes and the temper- ature in the lower parts of the Rivas, Brito and Masachapa formations is estimated at c. 120 uC. Mineralogical breaks are observed between the Masachapa and Brito formations as well as between the Brito and Rivas formations . These breaks were suggested to reﬂect tectonic events of regional character (Levi et al. 1990), possibly related to changes in the polarity of subduction. INTRODUCTION In order to improve the African palaeomagnetic database for Palaeozoic times, which is still poor, we have undertaken, during the last 10 years, systematic palaeomagnetic studies of the dated tabular formations of the Illizi basin (SE Algeria, Fig. 1a). Levels of various ages, ranging from the Silurian to the Albian, were analysed. These studies led to the determination of ﬁve new African palaeomagnetic poles. The ﬁrst, determined in the ‘El Adeb Larache’ area, is of Moscovian age (Henryet al. 1992), the second is of Stephano–Autunian age from the Tiguentourine For

, the third is from the Middle Zarzaı¨tine Formation of Liassic–Dogger age (Derder et al . 1994b), the fourth, determined in the ‘la Recule´e’ area from the Lower Zarzaitine is of Triassic–Liassic age (Kieset al. 1995), and the ﬁfth is of Bashkirian age from the Oubarakat Formation (Derder et al. 2001a). These studies also showed the existence of Cenozoic and Permian remagnetization events. However, as in most of the palaeomagnetic studies in hori- zontal tabular areas, the age of the magnetization acquisition has not been demonstrated. Indeed, in all cases, geological and geophysical constraints did not permit palaeomagnetic tests, except a reversal test in the Lower Zarzaı ¨tine Formation of Triassic–Liassic age (Kies et al. 1995). Such a reversal test is not absolute proof of the primary character of the magnetization, but indicates that the magnetization consists of a single com- ponent. The only argument in favour of the primary character of the magnetization is the variation of its direction from one formation to another, while the magnetic overprints (Permian and Cenozoic) observed at some levels have the same orientation in the different geological formations. To validate the previous results by a fold test, a new study was carried out 60 km SE of In Amenas city, in the Edjeleh region

INTRODUCTION In order to improve the African palaeomagnetic database for Palaeozoic times, which is still poor, we have undertaken, during the last 10 years, systematic palaeomagnetic studies of the dated tabular formations of the Illizi basin (SE Algeria, Fig. 1a). Levels of various ages, ranging from the Silurian to the Albian, were analysed. These studies led to the determination of ﬁve new African palaeomagnetic poles. The ﬁrst, determined in the ‘El Adeb Larache’ area, is of Moscovian age (Henryet al. 1992), the second is of Stephano–Autunian age from the Tiguentourine For

, the third is from the Middle Zarzaı¨tine Formation of Liassic–Dogger age (Derder et al . 1994b), the fourth, determined in the ‘la Recule´e’ area from the Lower Zarzaitine is of Triassic–Liassic age (Kieset al. 1995), and the ﬁfth is of Bashkirian age from the Oubarakat Formation (Derder et al. 2001a). These studies also showed the existence of Cenozoic and Permian remagnetization events. However, as in most of the palaeomagnetic studies in hori- zontal tabular areas, the age of the magnetization acquisition has not been demonstrated. Indeed, in all cases, geological and geophysical constraints did not permit palaeomagnetic tests, except a reversal test in the Lower Zarzaı ¨tine Formation of Triassic–Liassic age (Kies et al. 1995). Such a reversal test is not absolute proof of the primary character of the magnetization, but indicates that the magnetization consists of a single com- ponent. The only argument in favour of the primary character of the magnetization is the variation of its direction from one formation to another, while the magnetic overprints (Permian and Cenozoic) observed at some levels have the same orientation in the different geological formations. A palaeomagnetic study of the less deformed upper part of the Permian Tunas Formation of the Pillahuinco ´ region within the Sierras Australes belt was carried out in order to obtain reliable palaeomagnetic poles to constrain the palaeogeographic and tectonic evolution of this part of Gondwana. Palaeogeographically, these two Tunas Formation poles are interpreted as recording a slight counterclockwise movement of South America during the Permian. INTRODUCTION The southwestern margin of Gondwanaland was located north of the Colorado River during the Palaeozoic, and marks the boundary between the South America craton to the north and the Patagonia region to the south (Fig. 1). The Sierras Australes orogenic belt trends approximately NW–SE in the southwestern part of Buenos Aires province (Figs 1 and 2), and is considered to be the South American counterpart of the Cape Fold Belt in South Africa (Du Toit 1927). Its geological features have attracted the attention of many geologists since the early 1900s because it is a key to understanding the controversial evolution of this part of Gondwana. For some authors, the Sierras Australes are the result of intracontinental deformation exclusively (Selle´s Martı´nez 1989; Cobbold et al. 1991; Japas 1989); for others, the Sierras Australes are the result of the collision of the Patagonia terrane with Gondwana (Dalmayrac et al . 1980; Ramos 1984; Tomezzoli 1997). The deforma

alaeomagnetic study was to obtain additional reliable palaeomagnetic poles to evaluate the palaeogeographic and geo- dynamic evolution of this area, and therefore of Gondwana, building on the earlier study of Tomezzoli & Vilas (1999). Some investigators have suggested that there may have been more than one tectonic phase in this area, and postulated an early deformation phase of Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous age that preceded the widely recognized Upper Palaeozoic phase (Kilmurray 1975; Varela 1978; Ramos 1984, 1988; Tomezzoli 1997). Tomezzoli & Vilas (1999) reported the presence of a syn- tectonic magnetization carried by haematite (at 42 per cent unfolding) in the red sandstone and clay siltstone of the lower part of the Tunas Formation in the Sierra de las Tunas region (Fig. 2). They concluded that the lower part of the Tunas Formation was deformed and remagnetized very soon after its deposition in the Early Permian. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS We sampled oriented blocks, from which we cut from two to ﬁve oriented 8 cm 3 cubic samples. A total of 400 samples from different hand blocks were studied from 58 sites and 17 localities. Except for some Palaeozoic traps of the Viluy and Markha rivers, all directions were calculated using only in situ coordinates in the absence of any folding on the Siberian platform. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. Received 2001 June 13; in original form 2000 December 12 SUMMARY We studied basalt sills and dykes and kimberlite pipes from the eastern part of the Siberian platform. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation an

There is a belt of Early Triassic alkali–ultramaﬁc intrusions with carbonatites in the west of the Anabar Shield, younger than the Siberian traps (Zonenshain et al. 1990; Grifﬁn et al. 1999). For the present study, we sampled three Permo-Triassic trap sills (5–20 m thick) that overlie kimberlites or sediments in the areas of the Sytikanskaya, Yubileinaya and Aikhal pipes. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. Together with geological and absolute age data, the palaeomagnetic data support the hypothesis that kimberlite magmatism a

INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. The present study was intended to improve this situation and to contri- bute to the global palaeomagnetic database for one of the most * Present address: Physics Department, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada, T6G 2J1. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. A total of 400 samples from different hand blocks were studied from 58 sites and 17 localities. Except for some Palaeozoic traps of the Viluy and Markha rivers, all directions were calculated using only in situ coordinates in the absence of any folding on the Siberian platform. Stepwise thermal demagnetizations and magnetic measure- ments of the samples were carried out in the Irkutsk palaeo- magnetic laboratory (80 per cent of the samples) and in the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris (IPGP; 20 per cent of the samples). These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. Received 2001 June 13; in original form 2000 December 12 SUMMARY We studied basalt sills and dykes and kimberlite pipes from the eastern part of the Siberian platform. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation an

his ocean might have been related to ﬂood basalt magmatism. There is a belt of Early Triassic alkali–ultramaﬁc intrusions with carbonatites in the west of the Anabar Shield, younger than the Siberian traps (Zonenshain et al. 1990; Grifﬁn et al. 1999). For the present study, we sampled three Permo-Triassic trap sills (5–20 m thick) that overlie kimberlites or sediments in the areas of the Sytikanskaya, Yubileinaya and Aikhal pipes. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. There is a belt of Early Triassic alkali–ultramaﬁc intrusions with carbonatites in the west of the Anabar Shield, younger than the Siberian traps (Zonenshain et al. 1990; Grifﬁn et al. 1999). These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. Yubileinaya and Aikhal pipes. This is the most eastern occurrence of Permo-Triassic ﬂood basalts on the Siberian platform. Basalt dykes cut across Carboniferous– Permian sediments in our study region and their age is doubtlessly Permo-Triassic. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS We sampled oriented blocks, from which we cut from two to ﬁve oriented 8 cm 3 cubic samples. A total of 400 samples from different hand blocks were studied from 58 sites and 17 localities. Except for some Palaeozoic traps of the Viluy and Markha rivers, all directions were calculated using only in situ coordinates in the absence of any folding on the Siberian platform. Stepwise thermal demagnetizations and magnetic measure- ments of the samples were carried out in the Irkutsk palaeo- magnetic laboratory (80 per cent of the samples) and in the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris (IPGP; 20 per cent of the samples). Tables in this paper include two statistical levels: site averages based on samples and locality averages based on sites. Thermal demagnetization was performed in Irkutsk using ovens housed in three concentric m-metal shields. The residual ﬁeld is about 10 nT in the centre of the ovens. The samples were demagnetized in 10–50 uC steps up to 600–650 uC, and the remanent magnetization was measured

re demagnetized in 10–50 uC steps up to 600–650 uC, and the remanent magnetization was measured with a JR-4 spinner magnetometer. Magnetic susceptibility was measured with a KLY-2 Kappabridge (Irkutsk) and a Molspin susceptibility meter (Paris). In Paris, we used a Pyrox oven with about 4–6 nT residual ﬁeld, an alternating ﬁeld Schonstedt demagnetizer, a JR-5 spinner magnetometer and two-axis horizontal and vertical cryogenic magnetometers. Data were processed using Vinarsky et al.’s (1987) Opal software, Enkin’s (1996) palaeomagnetic data treatment software and the Cogne ´ (2000) Pa l e o M a c software. In all cases, Zijderveld (1967) diagrams were con- structed for each sample, results were analysed using principal component analysis (Kirschvink 1980), and site-mean directions were calculated using Fisher (1953) statistics. For mixed popu- lations of directions and remagnetization great circles with sector constraints (Halls 1976; McFadden & McElhinny 1988), we used the combined analysis technique of McFadden & McElhinny (1988). Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) experiments, thermomagnetic curves [Curie point measurements, J s(T)] and hysteresis loops were performed in the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Munich Institute of Applied Geophysics. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. Basalt dykes cut across Carboniferous– Permian sediments in our study region and their age is doubtlessly Permo-Triassic. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS We sampled oriented blocks, from which we cut from two to ﬁve oriented 8 cm 3 cubic samples. A total of 400 samples from different hand blocks were studied from 58 sites and 17 localities. Except for some Palaeozoic traps of the Viluy and Markha rivers, all directions were calculated using only in situ coordinates in the absence of any folding on the Siberian platform. Stepwise thermal demagnetizations and magnetic measure- ments of the samples were carried out in the Irkutsk palaeo- magnetic laboratory (80 per cent of the samples) and in the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris (IPGP; 20 per cent of the samples). These are spread out over a few hundred kilometres and are divided into two age groups: Late Permian–Early Triassic (Mir, Aikhal and Olenyek regions) and Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous (Viluy and Markha basins, Aikhal region). The palaeomagnetic poles determined for each sill or dyke are statistically different from each other, but averaging all corresponding directions from these sills and dykes with those from kimberlites of different generations yields results with acceptable statistics. This is probably due to the averaging out of secular variation and /or changes in magnetic polarity. The resulting palaeomagnetic poles allow one to reconstruct the palaeopositions of Siberia during the two large ﬂood basalt events at about 360 and 250 Ma. A signiﬁcant rotation of the Siberian platform during the Devonian and Carboniferous is suggested. The new data are in general agreement with some earlier palaeomagnetic poles for the Late Permian–Early Triassic traps of the Tungusska basin, and signiﬁcantly reduce uncertainties for previous Late Devonian–Early Carboniferous Siberian poles, which were very scattered. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. The present study was intended to improve this situation and to contri- bute to the global palaeomagnetic database for one of the most * Present address: Physics Department, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada, T6G 2J1. INTRODUCTION The kimberlites and Siberian trap formations have been studied palaeomagnetically in Siberia since 1963 (Savrasov & Kamisheva 1963; Davydov & Kravchinsky 1971; Kamysheva 1973; Zhitkov et al. 1994). This work was mainly intended to constrain the physical properties and the age of the kimberlites, because this problem was of interest to the Diamond Exploration Company ‘Almazy-Sakha-Rossija’. Although many palaeo- magnetic studies of Middle–Late Palaeozoic rocks have been performed in Siberia, most do not meet present-day reliability requirements. A direct consequence is that the apparent polar wander path (APWP) of the Siberian platform remains poorly constrained, thus there is a crucial need for new studies using modern techniques. The most recent compilations of the Siberian data (Van der Voo 1993; Smethurst et al. 1998) reveal large uncertainties for the Middle–Late Palaeozoic records. Ridgway Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907, USA ABSTRACT Volcanic and sedimentary strata of the Late Cretaceous MacColl Ridge Formation were sampled and demagnetized to reevaluate the paleomagnetically derived paleolatitude of the allochthonous Wrangellia terrane. Characteristic directions from 15 sites representing ;750 m of the MacColl Ridge Formation (80 Ma) reveal a reversed-polarity primary magnetization yielding a paleomagnetic pole at 126 8E, 688N, A 95 5 98. Comparison of this pole with the Late Cretaceous reference pole for North America indicates 15 86 88 of latitudinal displacement (northward) and 3386258 of counterclockwise rotation. In con- trast to previously reported low paleolatitudes (32 86 98N) for the MacColl Ridge For- mation, these new results place the Wrangellia terrane at a moderate paleolatitude (538 6 88N) in the Late Cretaceous. ences, University of Liverpool, Liverpool L69 3BX. SYNOPSIS Magnetic remanence is employed to date episodes of pseudotachylyte formation within the Lewisian terrane. In the Southern Zone on the mainland directions of magnetisation correlate with late stages of post-Laxfordian uplift and imply that these examples were either contemporaneous with the LM3 metamorphism or with early Torr- idonian rifting. In the Outer Hebrides the pseudotachylytes yield both mid-Proterozoic and Caledonian directions of magnetisation. The Proterozoic examples were formed late in the post-Laxfordian uplift cycle while the Palaeozoic examples are linked to formation of the Outer Hebrides thrust zone and presumably to the Caledonian thrusting on the mainland. The latter examples imply that differential uplift of the order of several kilometres has taken place between the Outer Hebrides and the Mainland since Caledonian times; their presence here explains why Torridonian and Lower Palaezoic cover rocks are not preserved in the former area. INTRODUCTION Pseudotachylytes, the flinty crush rocks generally attributed to frictional melting involving high strain rates during ancient seismic events, are found in two contrasting situations within the Lewisian metamorphic complex. Firstly, they are wide

irstly, they are widely present in the Outer Hebrides south of Harris within, and on either side of, the Outer Hebrides thrust zones; they occur here as ramifying veins ranging from microscopic in size up to several metres in thickness (Jehu and Craig 1924; Francis and Sibson 1973). Secondly, they are widely distributed within the Southern Zone on the mainland (Park 1961) in WNW trending crush belts formed after the main Laxfordian metamorphic events and pegmatite emplacement in this area (c. 1900- 1500 Ma), but prior to final uplift of the metamorphic complex and deposition of the overlying Torridonian sediments (c. 1000 Ma). Whilst formation of the mainland pseudotachylytes can be constrained to the interval c. 1500-1000 Ma from field evidence, the age of the Hebridean examples can only be dated between late Laxfordian events (c. 1500 Ma) and deposition of the Stornoway Beds of probable Permo-Triassic age (Storetvedt and Steel 1977). The evidence for a more precise age assignment is conflicting: the geometrical similarity of the Outer Hebrides thrust zone with the Caledonian thrusts on the mainland, the occasional preservation of glass, and some K/Ar age dates, all Scott. METHOD Owing to their fine grain size and variable alteration, pseudotachylytes are poor material for radiometric investigations. However, they generally possess a strong and stable remanent magnetism apparently because they contain abundant fine grains of ferromagnetic minerals in the single or pseudosingle domain size range (<30 jitm); these grains appear to have formed and acquired a magnetism in the ambient field over intervals of the order of seconds or minutes during which the pseudotachylytes chilled (Francis and Sibson 1973). Provided that this primary remanence can be recovered, the age of acquisition may be deduced by comparing the direction of magnetism with the predicted path of the palaeofield direction with respect to the sampling area between the time limits defined by geological evidence. This approach has been applied to the dating of pseudotachylyte formation in the Nagssugtoqidian mobile belt in East and West Greenland (Beckmann 1983, Piper 1981). Periods of both normal and transcurrent faulting have occurred on both faults. Many of the studies that give poles in the orogenic group are based on magnetizations that were demonstrably acquired penecontemporaneously with local folding events (Johnson and Van der Voo 1999), just like the ST2 magnetization in this study. In this situation, as noted by DiVenere and Opdyke (1991), the importance of defining exactly to which horizontal reference frame rota - tions are calculated becomes critical. This becomes essential when, as described by geological studies, the polarity of the half-grabens controlling sedimentation is changing both tem - porally and spatially (Hamblin and Rust 1989). The available evidence does not preclude the possibility of some lateral displacement. Many of the studies that give poles in the orogenic group are based on magnetizations that were demonstrably acquired penecontemporaneously with local folding events (Johnson and Van der Voo 1999), just like the ST2 magnetization in this study. In this situation, as noted by DiVenere and Opdyke (1991), the importance of defining exactly to which horizontal reference frame rota - tions are calculated becomes critical. This becomes essential when, as described by geological studies, the polarity of the half-grabens controlling sedimentation is changing both tem - porally and spatially (Hamblin and Rust 1989). It is very likely then that the observed discrepancy arises from unrecog- nized tilt acquired subsequent to remanence acquisition. Pole ST1 is widely divergent from most other Carboniferous poles. Such disparate directions are also known from other sectors of the Appalachian–Caledonide orogenic belt. Periods of both normal and transcurrent faulting have occurred on both faults. As a result, models for the development of the Stellarton Basin have included a pull-apart basin and a thermal subsidence basin. Paleomagnetic study of stratigraphic sequences from within the graben showed evidence for three separate periods of remanence acquisition (ST3 – ST2 – ST1). Ordering the acquisition sequence for these three magnetizations is mainly circumstantial, being based on the distribution of each remanence phase relative to stratigraphic position and deformation of the strata. The oldest magnetization ST3 is grossly divergent from previously reported Carboniferous results suggesting an early period of large-scale clockwise rotation. Magnetization ST2 has a similar pole position to many others from Maritime Carboniferous basins located within the Appalachian orogenic belt. We collected paleomagnetic samples from a total of 34 sites of the mid-Cretaceous Goshonoura Group, shallow- marine clastic deposits in west-central Kyushu, and characteristic remanent magnetizations were recognized from 18 horizons of red beds. HARRIS Earth Sciences, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario, Canada N9B 3P4 Abstract The Sherman-type Zn-Pb-Ag dolomite deposits in central Colorado are hosted in dolostones of the Early Mississippian Leadville Formation. Thermal demagnetization isolated characteristic remanent magnetization components with unblocking temperatures of 500–580 ◦C from all the sites. The Arima and Ikuno areas are 60 km apart from each other. 2 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING The Late Cretaceous Arima Group unconformably overlies the Jurassic–Early Cretaceous Tamba Group and the Early Cretaceous Sasayama Group, and is unconformably overlain by the Eocene – Oligocene Kobe Group. The Arima Group is well exposed in the Arima (34.8 ◦N, 135.3◦E) and Ikuno (35.2◦N, 134.7◦E) areas to the north of Kobe (Fig. 1b). It is made up mainly of rhyolitic lavas and pyroclastic rocks, and is divided into three parts (lower, middle and upper formations) (Kasama & Y oshida 1976; Nakazawa et al. 1987). The upper formation of the Arima Group is K –Ar dated at 72.1 ± 3.6 Ma (Y oshida & Kawada 1987). Tilting of the Arima Group occurred prior to the Eocene. In the Arima area, all the three formations are composed mainly of welded tuffs. Welded tuffs in the middle and upper forma- tions of the Arima area are rich in lithic fragments, whereas those in the lower formation rarely contain lithic fragments (Kasama & Y oshida 1976; Nakazawa et al. 1987). The Arima and Ikuno areas are 60 km apart from each other. 2 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND SAMPLING The Late Cretaceous Arima Group unconformably overlies the Jurassic–Early Cretaceous Tamba Group and the Early Cretaceous Sasayama Group, and is unconformably overlain by the Eocene – Oligocene Kobe Group. The Arima Group is well exposed in the Arima (34.8 ◦N, 135.3◦E) and Ikuno (35.2◦N, 134.7◦E) areas to the north of Kobe (Fig. 1b). It is made up mainly of rhyolitic lavas and pyroclastic rocks, and is divided into three parts (lower, middle and upper formations) (Kasama & Y oshida 1976; Nakazawa et al. 1987). The upper formation of the Arima Group is K –Ar dated at 72.1 ± 3.6 Ma (Y oshida & Kawada 1987). Tilting of the Arima Group occurred prior to the Eocene. In the Arima area, all the three formations are composed mainly of welded tuffs. Welded tuffs in the middle and upper forma- tions of the Arima area are rich in lithic fragments, whereas those in the lower formation rarely contain lithic fragments (Kasama & Y oshida 1976; Nakazawa et al. 1987). NEW MAGNETOSTRATIGRAPHIC RESULTS 3.1 Treatment The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the samples was measured using the 2G cryogenic magnetometer at the palaeomag- netic laboratory of the University of Kobe. The samples were sub- jected to progressive thermal and/or alternating ﬁeld demagneti- zation, using a laboratory built thermal demagnetizer and a Nat- suhara Giken AF demagnetizer. Principal component analysis was used to separate and calculate the different magnetic components (Kirschvink 1980), and site-mean directions were calculated using Fisher’s method (1953) or McFadden & McElhinny (1988) statistics. 3.2 Magnetic behaviour Thermal demagnetization was effectively used in a pilot study. section_candidates.excerpt: Abstract Early Palaeozoic volcanic and sedimentary rocks from the Saxothuringian Basin (Franconian Forest, northern Bavaria) have been subjected to detailed radio- metric and palaeomagnetic studies in order to determine the tectonic environment and geographic setting in which they were deposited. Paleomagnetic Results [15] We determined paleomagnetic remanence directions for 213 samples from 25 of the 27 sites; two sites were redundant and therefore not measured. We determined within-site mean remanence directions (‘‘site means’’) for 20 of these 25 sites (Table 1). Because of severe over- printing or large (>15 ) within-site scatter, we did not determine site means for the other five sites. [ 16] In the determination of the 20 usable site means, we discarded 20 of the 170 samples due to presumed large orientation errors (6 samples), unremovable isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) overprints (8 samples), or unstable demagnetization paths (6 samples). Orientation errors were invoked only for samples that had broken out of the outcrop before orientation and possessed a remanence direction more than three standard deviations away from the mean remanence direction for its site. IRM overprints, probably lightning-induced, were recognized through a combination of high natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensity, anomalous remanence direction, and a significant drop in NRM intensity at low (5 – 10 mT) applied alternating fields. Unstable demagnetization paths were those with repeated large and seemingly random changes in

Extrusive igneous rocks [ 17] We sampled 13 sites of extrusive rocks ranging in composition from mafic alkaline basalts and trachytes to silicic rhyolite lava flows and ash flows (ignimbrites and vitrophyres). Despite their age, most of these extrusives appear fresh and are stable and reliable paleomagnetic recorders. For 12 of these 13 sites, demagnetization behavior was straightforward, within-site dispersion is low, and the rock magnetic data indicate that titanomagnetite dominates the magnetic mineralogy. In the following discussion, the extrusive sites are divided into three groups according to their magnetic behavior, as the behavior in each group is consistent across lithology. [ 18] Sample magnetization data from sites 35, 36, 37, 38, 42, 53a, 53b, 54, and 55 are characterized by high stability components of magnetization that, after removal of minor secondary overprints, decayed linearly toward the origin during AF and thermal demagnetization (Figures 4a – 4b). Paleomagnetic Results [15] We determined paleomagnetic remanence directions for 213 samples from 25 of the 27 sites; two sites were redundant and therefore not measured. We determined within-site mean remanence directions (‘‘site means’’) for 20 of these 25 sites (Table 1). Because of severe over- printing or large (>15 ) within-site scatter, we did not determine site means for the other five sites. [ 16] In the determination of the 20 usable site means, we discarded 20 of the 170 samples due to presumed large orientation errors (6 samples), unremovable isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) overprints (8 samples), or unstable demagnetization paths (6 samples). Orientation errors were invoked only for samples that had broken out of the outcrop before orientation and possessed a remanence direction more than three standard deviations away from the mean remanence direction for its site. IRM overprints, probably lightning-induced, were recognized through a combination of high natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensity, anomalous remanence direction, and a significant drop in NRM intensity at low (5 – 10 mT) applied alternating fields. Unstable demagnetization paths were those with repeated large and seemingly random changes in both declination and inclination or those with increases in intensity as temperature or alternating field increased near the end of demagnetization of the sample. 4.1.1. [1] Paleomagnetic results from an Upper V endian sedimentary sequence exposed along the White Sea shoreline, NW Russia are described. These classical exposures have been the subject of intense paleontological investigations due to their well-preserved Ediacara fauna, but no paleomagnetic results have as yet been published. A total of 337 hand samples and 210 oriented drill cores (35 sites) along three profiles have been collected at the locality (65.5 , 40.0 E) where a 555 ± 3 Ma U–Pb age of comagmatic zircons from volcanic ash layers has been recently obtained. Standard paleomagnetic procedures yield two main natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components: an inte

= 23.3, a95 =4 . 8 , south pole position at 24 S, 132 E, dp = 2.3 ,d m= 3.8 ). This latter component, termed Z, passes reversal, stratigraphic, and consistency tests and is interpreted to reflect the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field during Late V endian times. This large oceanic plateau, with its conjugate Bro- ken Ridge, is a manifestation of intensive Cretaceous (119–95 Ma) volcanism due to the Kerguelen hotspot (Duncan, 2002 and references therein). The Kergue- len Archipelago represents the continuation of this hotspot volcanism for the last 30 Ma (Yang et al., 1998; Weis et al., 1998; Nicolaysen et al., 2000) ,b u t some magmatic contribution from the Southeast In- dian Ridge (SEIR) during the early Cenozoic is not excluded (Doucet et al., 2002).
